about.text: The complainant, Optimum Communications Services, Inc. (OCS), is a Delaware corporation based in Jersey City, New Jersey, that has developed and marketed the patented technology since 2001 through a predecessor company; Mark Sandstrom, OCS's president, is the named inventor on both patents at issue. The three proposed respondents—Hangzhou Softel Optic Co., Ltd., Hangzhou DAYTAI Network Technologies Co., Ltd., and Hangzhou Sumlo Industrial Co., Ltd.—are Chinese companies that manufacture, trade, or supply GPON OLT and ONU equipment for sale into North America.

The technology at issue is Dynamic Bandwidth Assignment (DBA), a method used in passive optical networks (xPON) to share fiber-optic bandwidth among multiple subscribers efficiently. DBA is used in standards such as GPON, 10GPON/XGS-PON, TWDM-PON/NG-PON2, and EPON/10G-EPON. The accused products are OLT (optical line termination) and ONU/ONT (optical network unit/terminal) devices—the hardware at each end of a fiber-optic network connection—that implement DBA under these standards, including Softel's OLT-G16 device. The complainant asserts U.S. Patent No. 7,558,260 (the '260 patent), covering a self-optimizing communications network using dynamic frame-slot assignment, and U.S. Patent No. 7,333,511 (the '511 patent), covering a network for transporting data based on dynamically channelizable buses; specifically claims 1 and 3 of the '260 patent and claims 1 and 12-14 of the '511 patent (claims are the numbered statements in a patent defining what it covers). The Commission instituted the investigation on infringement of these listed claims by OLT and ONU/ONT equipment conforming to the identified xPON standards.

allegations.text: OCS alleges that the accused respondents import their GPON/xPON OLT and ONU equipment into the United States through online marketplaces such as made-in-china.com, alibaba.com, and aliexpress.com, quoting prices in U.S. dollars and offering U.S. shipping; it alleges that Softel and DAYTAI have specifically confirmed their ability to ship such products to U.S. addresses.

OCS alleges infringement on the theory that the accused products implement the GPON standard (and successor xPON standards), and that claim charts show the standard itself requires the features recited in at least the first claim of each asserted patent; because xPON operation requires OLT and ONU equipment to work together, OCS alleges that importation of either type of device results in infringing implementation of the standard.

For its domestic industry requirement (the U.S. economic activity tied to the patented technology that a complainant must show to obtain relief under Section 337), OCS points to xPON-standard products and services it and its licensees provide, including the GPON-based municipal fiber network operated by EPB Fiber Optics in Chattanooga, Tennessee, which serves over 126,000 customers and represents roughly $220 million in network investment, with equipment-related domestic industry investment calculated at over $10 million.

OCS requests a general exclusion order (a Commission order barring imports of infringing products from any source, not just named respondents) or, alternatively, a limited exclusion order (barring imports only from the named respondents), together with cease and desist orders barring the sale, distribution, and marketing of infringing inventory already in the United States. OCS argues a general exclusion order is warranted because hundreds of corporate entities sell xPON equipment online under variable brand and importer names, including customizable labeling and subassembly components, making it impractical to identify all sources of infringing goods.

summary.headline: Optimum Communications Services, Inc. asked the Commission to bar imports of GPON and successor-standard passive optical network equipment—optical line termination (OLT) and optical network unit/terminal (ONU/ONT) devices—from Chinese suppliers Hangzhou Softel Optic, Hangzhou DAYTAI Network Technologies, and Hangzhou Sumlo Industrial, alleging the equipment's dynamic bandwidth assignment features infringe two of its patents.
